it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-01.question: What property makes a password fundamentally more resistant to automated guessing attacks?

options.a: It contains the department name, so it's easier to remember
options.b: It is long, unique to this one account, and not easy to guess
options.c: It is replaced every three days with a very similar password
options.d: It consists only of digits, because that speeds up typing

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-01.explanation: Length and uniqueness are the key factors against automated guessing and so-called credential stuffing, where stolen login data from other services is tried out. A password tied to the workplace is easy to guess, frequent changes to a very similar password bring little security benefit, and purely numeric passwords have far too few possible combinations.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-02.question: Why is multi-factor authentication (MFA) considered significantly more secure than a password alone?

options.a: Because it makes the password unnecessary and nothing needs to be remembered anymore
options.b: Because it fully protects the account against every kind of attack
options.c: Because even with a stolen password, an attacker would additionally need the second factor
options.d: Because it is technically only possible for administrator accounts

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-02.explanation: MFA combines something you know (a password) with something you have (e.g. an app or token) or something you are. A stolen password alone is then no longer enough for an attacker. MFA does not replace the password, does not offer complete protection against every type of attack, and today is available for practically any user account, not only administrator accounts.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-03.question: A colleague asks you to briefly use their personal user account and password because their own access is currently locked. How should you respond?

options.a: Decline, and instead inform IT support or the manager responsible
options.b: Agree, as long as it's only used briefly
options.c: Agree, but afterwards change the colleague's password yourself
options.d: Agree if the task is urgent and no other access seems possible

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-03.explanation: Accounts are tied to individuals so that actions in the system can be clearly attributed to one person (accountability). If an account is shared, it becomes impossible afterwards to determine who actually did what - which also makes investigating security incidents much harder. Urgency does not justify an exception; the correct path is to restore proper access through IT support.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-04.question: You leave your desk for a short conversation in the next office. What is the correct way to handle your unlocked computer?

options.a: Do nothing, since it's an internal office building
options.b: Lock the screen before leaving your workstation
options.c: Just close the open document, everything else can stay open
options.d: Turn off the monitor - that's enough protection

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-04.explanation: An unlocked computer lets anyone with brief access to the room - including visitors, cleaning staff, or unauthorised third parties - reach every open program and piece of data. Turning off the monitor changes nothing, since the session keeps running in the background. Locking the screen (e.g. via a keyboard shortcut) is a simple, effective baseline measure, regardless of how trustworthy the environment seems.

it_sicherheit-phishing-01.question: Which of the following is a typical warning sign of a phishing email?

options.a: The email arrives during normal working hours
options.b: The email includes the company logo as an attachment
options.c: The email creates time pressure and demands an immediate, unusual action
options.d: The email was sent to several colleagues at the same time

it_sicherheit-phishing-01.explanation: Attackers deliberately rely on artificial time pressure and emotional urgency so that recipients act immediately - clicking a link or handing over data - instead of pausing to think or checking with someone. Logos, normal sending times, or a wider recipient list say nothing on their own about whether a message is genuine, since logos are easily copied and send times or recipient lists can be chosen freely.

it_sicherheit-phishing-02.question: You receive an email apparently from senior management urgently and confidentially instructing you to transfer a large sum to a new, unfamiliar account. What is the correct first step?

options.a: Execute the transfer immediately, since instructions from senior management take priority
options.b: Verify the request personally through a known, independent channel (e.g. a phone call) before doing anything
options.c: Reply to the email and ask for written confirmation there
options.d: Make the transfer, but send a smaller amount than requested

it_sicherheit-phishing-02.explanation: This pattern is often called "CEO fraud": attackers impersonate a manager and exploit authority, confidentiality, and time pressure to bypass normal controls. Replying within the same email thread does not help, since the attacker controls exactly that channel. The key step is verification through an independent, already-known contact route - such as a call to a phone number on file - before any payment or action is carried out.

it_sicherheit-phishing-03.question: An email displays a link that supposedly leads to your company's known login page. What is the most sensible way to check whether the link is trustworthy without clicking it?

options.a: Hover the mouse over the link (without clicking) and check the actual destination address shown in the status bar
options.b: Click the link and then immediately check whether the page looks genuine
options.c: Check whether the email is written in correct German
options.d: Check the sender name shown in the display field of the email program

it_sicherheit-phishing-03.explanation: The displayed link text can differ completely from the actual destination address; only hovering with the mouse reveals the real URL in the browser's or email program's status bar. Clicking already carries risk, since some fake pages automatically load malicious code. Flawless language is no longer a reliable indicator, since phishing texts today often look very professional, and the displayed sender name can easily be forged without matching the actual sending address.

it_sicherheit-phishing-04.question: You clicked a link in a suspicious email and accidentally entered your login credentials there. What is the correct response?

options.a: Wait and see if anything unusual shows up in the account, and only react then
options.b: Do nothing, since it's probably a harmless one-off
options.c: Change the password in the next few days, whenever there's time
options.d: Change the password immediately and report the incident promptly to the responsible internal contact (e.g. IT security)

it_sicherheit-phishing-04.explanation: The faster compromised credentials are changed and the incident reported, the smaller the window in which an attacker can misuse the stolen data. Waiting, doing nothing, or delaying unnecessarily increases the risk, especially if the same password is also used for other systems. Reporting to the responsible contact also allows further protective measures to be taken and other staff to be warned.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-01.question: Why are regular, scheduled data backups important, even if a device is currently running reliably?

options.a: Because backups make passwords unnecessary
options.b: Because data can be lost through user error, technical failure, or malware such as ransomware, regardless of how reliable the device currently seems
options.c: Because backups are only required for very old devices
options.d: Because without a backup, the internet connection becomes slower

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-01.explanation: A backup protects against very different causes of data loss: accidental deletion, hardware failure, but also ransomware that encrypts files. A device's past reliability says nothing about future failures or attacks. Backups have nothing to do with passwords or internet speed and make sense regardless of a device's age.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-02.question: You find an unlabeled USB stick in the company parking lot. What is the correct way to handle it?

options.a: Plug it into a company computer to find out who it belongs to
options.b: Keep it and use it privately, since no one seems to be missing it
options.c: Do not connect it, and instead hand it over to the IT department or security staff
options.d: Check it on a personal device before deciding what to do

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-02.explanation: Unknown USB sticks are a classic entry point for malware: they can be prepared to automatically execute malicious code as soon as they are plugged in, even before any file is opened. This applies to company computers just as much as to personal devices. The safe approach is not to investigate the find yourself, but to hand it to the responsible department, which can examine it under controlled conditions.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-03.question: Why should you install security updates for the operating system and applications on your work device promptly when the system offers them?

options.a: Because updates often close known security vulnerabilities that could otherwise be exploited by attackers
options.b: Because updates mainly improve the look of the user interface
options.c: Because updates only increase the speed of the device
options.d: Because updates are only security-relevant on personally owned devices

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-03.explanation: Security vulnerabilities in operating systems and applications are continuously discovered and published; vendors close them through updates. If an update is postponed, the vulnerability remains open, and attackers frequently target exactly the period shortly after it becomes publicly known. Interface design or speed are at most side effects, not the real security reason, and update discipline applies to work devices just as much as to personal ones.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-04.question: A colleague recommends a handy, free add-on program from the internet for your company computer. What is the most sensible way to proceed?

options.a: Install it right away, since it's free and doesn't cost anything
options.b: Install it, but only on the computer, not on the work phone
options.c: Install it, as long as it's downloaded from a well-known website
options.d: Ask the responsible IT department beforehand whether and how the software can be approved

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-04.explanation: Unapproved software can contain security vulnerabilities, conflict with other programs, or violate licensing and compliance rules - regardless of whether it's free, which website it comes from, or what type of device it's installed on. The IT department can check whether software can be used safely and in line with policy, and can provide a vetted alternative if needed.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-01.question: Which measure contributes most to securing the home Wi-Fi network for work purposes in a home-office setting?

options.a: Setting the Wi-Fi network name (SSID) so it sounds inconspicuous
options.b: Using a strong, individual Wi-Fi password and up-to-date encryption (e.g. WPA2/WPA3)
options.c: Only turning the Wi-Fi on during the day and switching it off completely at night
options.d: Keeping the router's factory-default access settings unchanged to avoid mistakes

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-01.explanation: A strong, individual password together with modern encryption prevents unauthorised people within range from simply joining the network and reading or tampering with traffic. An inconspicuous network name provides no technical protection, switching the Wi-Fi off at times doesn't solve the underlying problem, and factory-default settings (default passwords, default SSID) are often publicly known and therefore especially insecure.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-02.question: You need to quickly check work email while out and about, and find an open, unencrypted Wi-Fi network in a café. What is the safest way to proceed?

options.a: Use the open Wi-Fi directly, since checking email is low-risk
options.b: Use the open Wi-Fi, but change your own password beforehand
options.c: Instead of the open Wi-Fi, use a secured connection, such as mobile data or a company VPN
options.d: Use the open Wi-Fi, as long as the café's website shows a padlock icon in the address bar

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-02.explanation: In open, unencrypted Wi-Fi networks, traffic can be intercepted or redirected by others on the same network, even if individual websites are themselves encrypted (the padlock icon only covers that one connection, not the whole network). Mobile data or a company VPN establishes an additionally secured, encrypted connection that is far harder to intercept. Changing your password beforehand does not address the actual risk.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-03.question: You are working on a confidential document on your laptop on a train. What should you keep in mind to prevent others from reading over your shoulder?

options.a: Stay aware of your surroundings and, if needed, use a privacy screen filter or a seating position that limits visibility
options.b: Just zoom the document out smaller so it can't be read from a distance
options.c: Only anonymise the file name, since the content itself isn't sensitive
options.d: Generally treat confidential documents on the go the same as publicly available information

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-03.explanation: "Shoulder surfing" - other people reading a screen over someone's shoulder - is a real risk in public settings like trains or waiting areas. A privacy screen filter or a well-chosen seating position effectively reduces this risk. Zooming out smaller is not a reliable protection, the file name is not the actual thing that needs protecting, and confidential content always needs appropriate protection regardless of location, not just in the office.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-04.question: You are traveling for work and need to briefly leave your company laptop in a parked car. What is the safest way to handle this?

options.a: Leave the laptop clearly visible on the passenger seat so it isn't forgotten
options.b: Place the laptop in the not-visible trunk and lock the vehicle, or preferably take it with you entirely
options.c: Hide the laptop under a jacket on the back seat - that's enough protection
options.d: It doesn't matter, as long as the laptop is protected by a user password

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-04.explanation: Visible valuables in a car significantly increase the risk of a break-in; a not-visible trunk or taking the device along noticeably reduces this risk. A jacket used as visual cover is unreliable and does not protect against a targeted break-in. A user password partly protects the data on the device if it is stolen, but does not prevent the physical loss of the device itself, and therefore does not replace secure storage.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-01.question: You suspect your company computer may be infected with malware, but you're not entirely sure. How should you behave?

options.a: Wait until there is clear proof, so as not to raise a false alarm
options.b: Report the suspicion promptly to the responsible internal contact (e.g. IT security or the helpdesk), even if you're unsure
options.c: Reinstall the computer yourself and then carry on working as normal
options.d: First ask colleagues whether they've noticed anything similar before reporting anything

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-01.explanation: A functioning reporting and response culture requires that even mere suspicions are reported early, rather than waiting for clear proof - the sooner a possible incident becomes known, the better any spread can be contained. Re-installing the computer yourself can destroy important traces needed to determine the cause. Informally asking colleagues first also delays the report unnecessarily and does not replace informing the responsible contact.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-02.question: Why does the EU Network and Information Security Directive (NIS2) set such short deadlines for the initial report of a significant security incident (roughly: an early warning within hours, followed by a more detailed report)?

options.a: So that organisations gain as much time as possible to keep the incident quiet internally
options.b: Because a full technical investigation is never possible anyway
options.c: So that responsible authorities can respond early and other potentially affected organisations can be warned in time
options.d: Because short deadlines apply only to IT service providers, not to their customers

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-02.explanation: Short reporting deadlines exist to ensure authorities and other affected parties are informed quickly, so that a spread can be contained and countermeasures coordinated - not to enable internal cover-ups. An initial early report is deliberately allowed to be incomplete and is followed up later; that is exactly the point of a staged reporting process. The reporting obligations apply to affected organisations as a whole, not only to IT service providers.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-03.question: Why does a good security culture require employees to report a suspected security incident instead of trying to quietly fix it themselves?

options.a: Because an individual often cannot see the full scope and cause of an incident, and acting alone can erase evidence or make the problem worse
options.b: Because fixing it yourself is fundamentally a copyright violation
options.c: Because that's the only way to reduce a company's IT security costs
options.d: Because without reporting, employees are automatically made personally liable

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-03.explanation: A single incident can be part of a larger pattern - for example, an attack affecting several systems. Someone who tries to solve the problem alone, without reporting it, can destroy important evidence needed to determine the cause, and risks letting the incident spread unnoticed. The other listed reasons (copyright, cost reduction, automatic personal liability) do not describe the actual rationale behind the reporting requirement.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-04.question: You're unsure who in the company is responsible for reporting a suspected IT security incident. What is the most sensible approach?

options.a: Post about the incident in a public internal chat channel so that someone sees it
options.b: Wait until someone else happens to notice the problem and reports it
options.c: Describe the incident on social media to get quick attention
options.d: Use the company's established reporting channels (e.g. IT support, security officer, or line manager), or ask your own manager if in doubt

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-04.explanation: A prepared reporting process with clearly responsible contacts ensures an incident reaches the right people quickly, so appropriate countermeasures can be taken. A public chat channel or social media are unsuitable and could additionally make the incident public or tip off attackers. Waiting delays the response unnecessarily; when in doubt, your own manager is always a sensible first point of contact for finding the correct reporting channel.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-05.question: Why should employees only receive the access rights they actually need for their specific task (the "least privilege" principle)?

options.a: So that fewer passwords need to be managed
options.b: So that if an account is compromised or a mistake happens, the possible damage stays limited to what's necessary
options.c: So that the IT department has fewer support requests to handle
options.d: So that all employees hold exactly the same amount of rights and no one is disadvantaged

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-05.explanation: The least-privilege principle limits the damage a stolen account or an accidental mistake can cause, because access is restricted to only the systems and data actually needed. It is not about the number of passwords, support workload, or formal equal treatment, but about limiting risk according to each person's actual task.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-06.question: A colleague moves internally to a different department with different tasks. What should happen to her previous system access?

options.a: Nothing, since she is still working for the same company
options.b: The previous access stays in place in addition to the new access, so she can flexibly help out
options.c: Access rights that are no longer needed are withdrawn and permissions are adjusted to match the new role
options.d: Only the password is changed, the rights themselves stay the same

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-06.explanation: Permissions should match a person's current responsibilities; when someone changes roles, access rights that are no longer required must be withdrawn and new, appropriate rights granted. Otherwise unnecessary, excessive permissions accumulate over time ("privilege creep"), needlessly increasing the risk if the account is ever compromised. Simply changing the password does not address this.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-07.question: You need to remember many different passwords for work systems. What is the most sensible approach?

options.a: Use a password manager approved by IT, instead of reusing passwords or writing them down unprotected
options.b: Use the same easy-to-remember password for every system
options.c: Write the passwords on a sticky note on the monitor so they're quick to find
options.d: Store the passwords in an unencrypted text file on the desktop

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-07.explanation: An approved password manager makes it possible to use a long, unique password for every system without having to memorise each one individually, and it protects the stored credentials itself through encryption. Reusing passwords means a single data breach endangers every affected account; sticky notes and unencrypted files are immediately visible to anyone with physical or digital access.

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-08.question: You leave your desk in an open-plan office at the end of the day. What does the clear-desk principle require?

options.a: Only locking the screen, documents can be left lying out
options.b: Confidential documents may stay out in the open as long as the office door is locked
options.c: Only documents specifically marked "secret" need to be put away
options.d: Locking away confidential documents and storage media and leaving the desk tidy

it_sicherheit-zugriffsschutz-08.explanation: The clear-desk principle requires locking away confidential paper documents and storage media whenever you are away, so they are not freely accessible to unauthorised people - such as cleaning staff, visitors, or other employees without the right permissions. A locked office door alone does not protect against everyone with access to the building or room, and the rule applies to confidential documents in general, not only ones explicitly marked "secret".

it_sicherheit-phishing-05.question: You receive an email with an unexpected invoice attachment asking you to allow "macros" or "enable content" in order to view the invoice. What is the most sensible response?

options.a: Allow the macros, otherwise the invoice can't be opened
options.b: Open the attachment, but only after restarting the computer first
options.c: Do not enable macros, and have the email checked through the usual reporting channels if unsure
options.d: Forward the attachment to a colleague privately so they open it first

it_sicherheit-phishing-05.explanation: The request to enable macros is a well-known attack pattern: only enabling them executes malicious code contained in the file, which would otherwise remain inactive. Restarting the computer changes nothing, and forwarding it to a colleague only shifts the risk instead of removing it. If there is any doubt about the sender or content, the email should be checked through the usual internal reporting channels before anything is opened or enabled.

it_sicherheit-phishing-06.question: What distinguishes "spear phishing" from a classic, broadly scattered phishing campaign?

options.a: Spear phishing is carried out exclusively by phone, never by email
options.b: Spear phishing is tailored to a specific person or organisation and uses deliberately researched, credible details
options.c: Spear phishing never uses links or attachments at all
options.d: Spear phishing only ever targets private email accounts, never work accounts

it_sicherheit-phishing-06.explanation: In spear phishing, attackers deliberately research information about a person or organisation - such as managers' names, ongoing projects, or internal processes - to make a message appear especially credible and personally relevant. This makes such attacks harder to spot than generic mass phishing emails. Neither the communication channel, the absence of links/attachments, nor a restriction to private accounts is the defining feature.

it_sicherheit-phishing-07.question: You receive an SMS that supposedly comes from a parcel delivery service, with a link for a "customs fee payment", even though you're not expecting a parcel. How do you classify this and how do you respond?

options.a: This is likely "smishing" (phishing via SMS); do not click the link, and instead check the shipment directly via the delivery service's official website or app
options.b: SMS messages can generally not be faked, so the link is safe
options.c: Since it's a private text message, this topic has nothing to do with work and can be ignored
options.d: Click the link, but don't enter any payment details, just to see if it's a real shipment

it_sicherheit-phishing-07.explanation: Phishing is not limited to email: "smishing" uses text messages with the same underlying pattern of urgency and a manipulated link. An SMS sender name can also be spoofed. It is safer to check the supposed situation independently via the official website or app rather than following the link. This is also relevant for employees, since the same patterns can affect work devices or contact details, and merely clicking a manipulated link can already carry risk.

it_sicherheit-phishing-08.question: An email appears to come from "support@your-company-online.com", even though the actual company domain is "yourcompany.com". How should this slightly different sender domain most likely be interpreted?

options.a: As an insignificant typo with no security relevance
options.b: As a possible sign of a fake, deceptively similar domain ("typosquatting") used to mislead the recipient
options.c: As confirmation that the message is guaranteed to come from your own IT department
options.d: As simply a stylistic choice of domain made by the actual sender

it_sicherheit-phishing-08.explanation: Attackers deliberately register domains that closely resemble the real company domain (e.g. extra words, swapped letters, or different endings) to create false trust. Such a discrepancy is a serious warning sign, not a trivial detail or a matter of taste. If something looks off, the actual sender address should be checked carefully and, if in doubt, verified through an independent channel rather than assuming it is genuine.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-05.question: Why is it not enough, as protection against ransomware, to store a backup directly on the same permanently connected network drive as the original data?

options.a: Because network drives are technically always slower than local hard drives
options.b: Because backups are generally not allowed to be stored on network drives
options.c: Because ransomware can also encrypt a permanently connected backup drive along with the original data
options.d: Because network drives are exclusively meant for storing emails

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-05.explanation: Ransomware typically encrypts every reachable drive, including permanently connected network drives - a backup stored there then offers no real protection, since it can be affected as well. An effective backup concept therefore includes at least one copy kept separate (offline or with a time gap) from the production system, so it is not caught up in an attack on the main system.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-06.question: A backup is automatically created every night as scheduled. Why is that alone not yet enough to genuinely rely on the data backup?

options.a: Because it must be checked regularly whether data can actually be successfully restored from the backup
options.b: Because a backup should generally only be created once a year
options.c: Because automatic backups can technically never fail
options.d: Because a completed backup only remains valid for a maximum of 24 hours

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-06.explanation: A backup run can fail or produce a corrupted, incomplete copy without this being immediately noticed. Only a regular restore test reliably shows whether data can actually be recovered in an emergency. The backup frequency itself depends on need and isn't limited to once a year, automated processes can indeed fail, and a backup does not automatically become invalid after 24 hours.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-07.question: You want to transport confidential company data on an external USB storage device. What is the most important protective measure for this?

options.a: Put a noticeable "confidential" sticker on the device so it doesn't get misplaced
options.b: Encrypt the storage device, so the data cannot easily be read if it is lost or stolen
options.c: Choose a device that is as small and inconspicuous as possible so it doesn't stand out
options.d: Simply rename the files before copying them so their content isn't immediately obvious

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-07.explanation: Removable storage media are easily lost or stolen; without encryption, the data on them is then immediately readable by anyone with physical access. Encryption ensures the data stays protected even if the device is lost, as long as the key or password remains secret. A sticker, an inconspicuous form factor, or renamed files, by contrast, provide no real technical protection against unauthorised reading.

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-08.question: An old company laptop is to be decommissioned and disposed of. What is the correct approach regarding the data stored on it?

options.a: Just delete the visible files in the recycle bin and empty it
options.b: Pass the laptop on unchanged to a charity second-hand market to save resources
options.c: Remove the hard drive and throw it out with household waste
options.d: Have the responsible IT department securely and irrecoverably erase the data (or have the storage medium properly destroyed) before the device is passed on or disposed of

it_sicherheit-datensicherung-08.explanation: Simply deleting files in the recycle bin or formatting a drive usually only removes files from the visible directory, while the actual data often remains recoverable with suitable tools. Before a device is passed on or disposed of, its storage media must therefore be securely erased (e.g. by overwriting multiple times) or physically destroyed, so confidential company data does not end up in the wrong hands. Throwing it out with household waste is also not permitted for environmental and disposal reasons.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-05.question: Why is full-disk encryption on a laptop used for home-office work and business travel especially important?

options.a: Because it automatically makes the laptop boot faster
options.b: Because if the device is stolen or lost, it prevents unauthorised people from simply accessing the stored data
options.c: Because it is only required for devices that never leave the office
options.d: Because it makes a login password completely unnecessary

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-05.explanation: Devices used outside the office face a higher risk of theft or loss - for example on a train, in a car, or while travelling to a client. Without full-disk encryption, the built-in drive can often be removed and the data read directly, regardless of the operating system's login password. Encryption and a login password complement each other but do not replace one another, and none of this has anything to do with boot speed.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-06.question: Why should a short automatic screen lock (e.g. after 30 seconds of inactivity) be enabled on a smartphone used for work?

options.a: So the device is not immediately unprotected and accessible if briefly left unattended or lost
options.b: So the device's battery lasts longer
options.c: So calls are automatically muted
options.d: Because a screen lock is legally required only for phones used by senior management

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-06.explanation: A short lock interval reduces the window in which a briefly unattended or lost device can be used without authentication, for example to access email, contacts, or company apps. Battery life and call settings have no security relevance here, and the rule sensibly applies to all devices used for work, not only to a specific group of people.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-07.question: You occasionally use your personal smartphone for work purposes ("Bring Your Own Device"). What is most important to consider here from a security perspective?

options.a: Mixing private and work data as much as possible within the same apps, so nothing gets lost
options.b: It's enough that the device has some password, regardless of any further requirements
options.c: Complying with the organisation's BYOD policy (e.g. minimum protective measures, separation of work data, remote-wipe capability) before using the device for work
options.d: BYOD rules are purely voluntary and don't need to be followed as long as the device was privately purchased

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-07.explanation: When personal devices are used for work, the same protection goals as for company devices must be achieved - for example through minimum requirements for encryption, screen lock, separated areas for work data, and the ability to remotely wipe work data if the device is lost. Mixing private and work data undermines exactly this protection, and neither an arbitrary password alone nor the fact that the device was privately purchased exempts anyone from the organisation's applicable rules.

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-08.question: You join a work video conference from home where confidential matters are discussed. What should you pay particular attention to?

options.a: The screen can stay visible to housemates without any issue, as long as no one is actively reading along
options.b: That housemates, family members, or devices with voice assistants cannot overhear or see the confidential content
options.c: Only that the internet connection is fast enough for video
options.d: It's enough to turn off the camera; the microphone doesn't matter in this context

it_sicherheit-mobil_homeoffice-08.explanation: In a home environment, other people can also become aware of what's on screen or audible through the microphone - such as family members or visitors - and nearby voice-assistant devices could unintentionally pick up audio too. A quiet, shielded location and deliberate handling of screen and microphone protect confidentiality. Connection speed alone affects quality, not confidentiality, and muting the microphone is at least as important as the camera for spoken confidential content.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-05.question: What does the staged reporting timeline of the NIS2 Directive for a significant security incident roughly look like?

options.a: A single, complete report is enough, no later than one year after the incident
options.b: An early warning within 24 hours, a more detailed incident notification within 72 hours, followed by a final report no later than one month after the notification
options.c: Only a final report, which must be fully completed within 24 hours of the incident
options.d: A report is only required once an incident has already become publicly known

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-05.explanation: NIS2 provides for a staged process: an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware, a more detailed notification within 72 hours, and a final report no later than one month after that notification. This staging allows for a fast initial response even when not all details are yet known. A single report after one year, a fully complete report required within 24 hours, or waiting until an incident becomes public do not match the actual procedure.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-06.question: What basic idea does the NIS2 Directive use to determine whether a security incident counts as "significant" and therefore falls under the reporting obligation?

options.a: Whether the incident causes (or is capable of causing) severe operational disruption or financial loss, or considerably damages (or is capable of damaging) other persons or organisations
options.b: Whether the incident affects only the IT department itself, regardless of its actual scale
options.c: Whether the incident lasts longer than one working week, regardless of its impact
options.d: Whether the incident happens to occur during core working hours

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-06.explanation: Under NIS2, an incident is in particular considered significant if it causes, or is capable of causing, severe operational disruption or financial loss to the affected organisation, or if it considerably damages, or is capable of damaging, other natural or legal persons. Neither the mere fact that the IT department is affected nor the duration or time of day of the incident is, on its own, the decisive criterion - what matters is the actual or potential scale of impact.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-07.question: You suspect an ongoing security incident on your company computer. Why should you not restart or completely shut down the device on your own before reporting the incident?

options.a: Because restarting always uses more power than leaving the device running
options.b: Because restarting automatically deletes all company data on the device
options.c: Because doing so can lose volatile evidence (e.g. in memory) that is important for later investigating the incident
options.d: Because restarting automatically fixes the incident, making a report unnecessary

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-07.explanation: Some important traces of an incident - such as active network connections or processes in memory - are lost on restart or shutdown and cannot be reconstructed afterwards. For later root-cause analysis it is therefore important to leave the system as unchanged as possible and report the incident first, so the responsible team can decide on next steps. A restart does not automatically delete company data, nor does it fix any underlying security incident.

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-08.question: What information is particularly helpful when reporting a suspected IT security incident to the responsible internal contact?

options.a: Only your own name, since anything else just delays the report unnecessarily
options.b: As short a report as possible, without any timing information, so it can be sent quickly
options.c: Only a rough guess as to who might be responsible for the incident
options.d: As precise details as possible about the time, the observed anomalies, and the affected systems or data

it_sicherheit-meldepflicht_it-08.explanation: Concrete details about the time, the observed behaviour (e.g. unusual pop-ups, unexplained file changes), and the affected systems or data help the responsible team quickly assess the incident, estimate its scope, and initiate suitable countermeasures. Your name alone is not sufficient, a report without timing information makes it harder to establish a timeline, and speculating about "who is to blame" is not the decisive point for the technical handling of the incident.
